newsitem.title: USA: Senator seeks bar on business with Sudan, Syria.
newsitem.headline: Senator seeks bar on business with Sudan, Syria.

text.p: The head of the U.S. Senate panel that monitors Africa policy on Thursday joined moves in the House of Representatives to bar U.S. firms from doing business with Syria and Sudan because of their alleged links to terrorism.

Sen. John Ashcroft, a Missouri Republican, said at a hearing of his Foreign Relations subcommittee on Africa that he planned to sponsor a companion bill to plug a legal loophole that let U.S. companies pursue oil and other deals in the two countries.

At issue was the Clinton administration's interpretation of the 1996 Anti-Terrorism Act which, as enacted, barred financial transactions with the seven countries branded by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism -- Syria and Sudan as well as North Korea, Cuba, Iran, Libya and Iraq.

After President Bill Clinton signed the Anti-Terrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act into law on April 24, 1996, administration officials exempted Syria, citing Middle East peace imperatives, and Sudan, without citing a specific rationale.

The exemption let Occidental Petroleum Corp. pursue a $930 million deal in Sudan. The company later announced it was no longer interested in the deal, which involved a concession in the civil war-torn south, because, it said, the two sides were "too far apart on commercial terms."

"I am amazed that we are having to revisit this anti-terrorism legislation to force the president of the United States to cut off financial transactions with state sponsors of terrorism," Ashcroft said.
A bill that would strip the administration's authority to issue regulations exempting transactions from the ban on dealings with countries on the terrorism list was already moving through the House.

"I realise that this legislation could affect many law-abiding U.S. companies doing business in the affected countries," Representative Bill McCollum, a Florida Republican who is an author of the House measure, told the hearing.

"But in my view, the only way we are going to eliminate the governmental support terrorist organisations desperately need is to take a firm stance against economic relationships with these countries," said McCollum, who chairs both the House subcommittee on crime and an Intelligence Committee panel on spies and counterspies.

The assistant secretary of state for Africa, George Moose, told the hearing that the United States was seeking to isolate the Islamic fundamentalist government in Sudan so long as it provided safe havens to "terrorist" groups.

But he cautioned against "one-size-fits-all" legislative bans that he said could straitjacket U.S. diplomacy. He declined comment on the possible impact of any such move on Syria's stance on the U.S.-sponsored Arab-Israeli peace talks, which are stalled. He said the adminstration had not formulated its position on efforts to bar transactions other than those needed to conduct routine diplomacy.

Sudan's trade with the United States totalled only about $30 million each way, Kenneth McKune, the State Department's acting coordinator for counterterrorism, told the hearing. Two-way trade between the United States and Syria, mostly involving oil equipment and farm products, totals about $250 million, State Department officials said.
